::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**No behavior below has been observed in Positron.** The documentation claims
come from Posit pages read through a web fetch and carry ⚠️ on
[the references page](references.qmd). Two settings files from this group were
read on disk and carry ✅. Section 11 lists the checks outstanding. The finding
in Section 6 is the one to read first.
:::

## 1. Scope

One file, `.posit/assistant/settings.json`, committed to a project repository,
that lets the assistant work in the repository without a confirmation click on
every edit, and stops it from doing damage that version control cannot undo.

The reader is a statistician or pharmacometrician using Positron with the
assistant turned on. Section 4 explains agent permission systems from zero.

**Out of scope.** Model and provider comparison, prompting, and Posit Workbench
administration. This document also does not make the assistant safe to point at
identifiable patient data, and Section 10 says why no settings file can.

**A note on the name.** Positron Assistant and Databot merged into Posit
Assistant, which shipped as the default in Positron 2026.07. Both names are in
circulation. The setting that turns it on is now `assistant.enabled`, gated by
`ai.enabled`. The older `positron.assistant.enable` applies only before 2026.07.

## 2. The Recommendation

Set the approval mode to `auto`, allow `executeCode`, and write nothing else.

```json
{
  "approvalMode": "auto",
  "permission": {
    "executeCode": "allow"
  }
}
```

**`approvalMode: auto`** lets the assistant read, edit, run, build and commit
inside the project without asking, and gates everything that leaves it.
Section 5 compares it against the `normal` default.

**`executeCode: allow`** covers running R or Python in the active console
session. That is the tool this group uses most, it is separate from `bash`, and
no `bash` rule constrains it.

The file lives in the project root and is committed, so everyone working in the
repository gets the same posture. A personal file at
`~/.posit/assistant/settings.json` is overridden by it. Both paths were
confirmed on disk on 2026-09-12.

**⚠️ One thing here is unverified.** Whether `approvalMode` is accepted in a
project-level file or only globally. The check takes a minute and is question 1
in Section 11.

## 3. The Test That Keeps the File Short

Before writing any rule, ask whether git can undo the thing the rule prevents.
Almost nothing survives that question.

| Risk | Can git undo it | Rule needed |
|---|---|---|
| A file deleted, overwritten or mangled inside the project | Yes, to the last commit | No |
| A model definition or dependency list changed by mistake | Yes, to the last commit | No |
| Anything written outside the working directory | No | No, `auto` gates it |
| Credentials sent to an external endpoint | No | No, `auto` blocks it |
| A force-push | No | No, `auto` blocks it |
| Data sent to the model provider | No | None exists, see Section 6 |

Every row is either recoverable or already handled, which is why the file in
Section 2 has two settings.

**The habit carries the configuration.** Everything inside the project is
recoverable to the last commit and nothing before it. Uncommitted work is the
only project material a mistake can destroy permanently, and no setting in this
document protects it. An assistant in `auto` mode makes more changes per hour
than one asking permission, so the commits have to get more frequent to match.

## 4. How the Permission System Works

The assistant does not edit a file or run a command directly. It proposes a
**tool call**, a named request such as "edit `model.R`" or "run
`quarto render`". A permission layer answers each proposal with `allow`, which
runs it silently, `ask`, which shows a dialog, or `deny`, which refuses and
tells the assistant it was refused.

Each tool has a key used in the settings file.

| Key | What it governs |
|---|---|
| `executeCode` | Running R or Python in the active console session |
| `bash` | Shell commands, matched as patterns |
| `edit` | Changing or creating a file, matched per file pattern |
| `read` | Reading a file |
| `external_directory` | Any path outside the working directory |
| `webfetch` | Retrieving a URL, including an intranet address |
| `task` | Spawning a subagent, by type |
| `skill` | Invoking a named skill |

The remaining keys are `glob`, `grep`, `list`, `websearch`, `todowrite`,
`question`, `lsp` and `doom_loop`. None needs a rule in a pharmacometrics
project.

Both `bash` and `edit` take patterns, so `"git *": "allow"` and
`"rm *": "deny"` can sit side by side. A tool can also take one answer for
everything, written as `"read": "allow"`.

A `deny` is documented as absolute: no approval, mode or setting gets past it,
including in `auto` and `yolo`. That makes a written denial the strongest thing
available, on the rare occasion one is needed.

The **approval mode** answers everything the written rules do not mention,
which under the recommendation in Section 2 is everything.

## 5. Auto Against Normal

Four modes exist. `restricted` is for a repository you did not write and do not
trust. `yolo` removes the classifier and Section 10 is the argument against it.
The real choice is between the two in the middle.

| | `normal`, the default | `auto`, recommended |
|---|---|---|
| Who judges a risky tool call | You, in a dialog box | A classifier model reading the call |
| What the judgment uses | A fixed split of operations into safe and risky | The command, the path it touches, and the context |
| Where the boundary sits | Wherever accumulated approvals have put it | The working directory, plus a fixed blocked list |
| Is the decision written down | Yes, if you choose "for this project" | No |
| Prompts per hour | Many at first, fewer over time | Few, and the number does not drift |

`auto` allows what stays inside the working directory: reading and editing
files, running tests and builds, committing to the current branch, and
read-only web requests. It blocks a published list: piping a remote script into
an interpreter, sending credentials to an external endpoint, force-pushing, and
modifying production infrastructure. `normal` publishes no equivalent list.

**✅ Choose `auto`, and the reason is drift rather than convenience.** The
dialog in `normal` offers "allow for this project", which writes a permanent
entry into the settings file. After a few weeks that file is an allowlist
nobody designed, and it only ever grows. On day one `normal` is stricter than
`auto`. On day sixty it is looser, because its boundary has moved to wherever
the clicking put it, while the `auto` boundary has not moved at all.

A dialog that appears many times a day also stops being read.

**The floor of `auto` is `normal`.** If the classifier blocks three tool calls
in a row, the session drops back to `normal` and starts prompting. A session
that suddenly asks permission for everything has been demoted, and the thing to
look at is what the assistant was trying to do when it was blocked.

**Neither mode documents what it does with `rm -rf`.** Deletion is not on the
`auto` blocked list, so a recursive delete inside the working directory is
inside the zone the mode allows, and one outside it is gated for crossing the
boundary rather than for being destructive. A written
`"bash": {"rm -rf *": "deny"}` would hold, since a deny is absolute. It is not
recommended, because it guards a case git already covers and matches one
spelling out of several. `rm -fr`, `rm -r -f` and `unlink(recursive = TRUE)` in
the R console are all different strings.

## 6. What the Assistant Sends Without Being Asked

Posit Assistant attaches context to a chat turn automatically, and the list
includes the contents of the R or Python session.

- The file open in the active editor.
- The console history, both the code entered and the output it printed.
- The in-memory objects and data frames shown in the Variables pane.
- The current plot.
- The project structure and its version control history.

The setting `assistant.aiExcludes` takes glob patterns in the style of a
`.gitignore` file and excludes matching **files** from completions and chat
context.

**⚠️ Excluding a data file may not exclude the data.** The documentation
describes `aiExcludes` as operating on file contents and describes the
Variables pane as a separate context source. Read literally, a data frame built
from an excluded CSV file still reaches the provider once it is in memory.
Untested, and it is question 2 in Section 11.

**❌ Do not point the assistant at a session holding identifiable patient data
until that check is done.** A settings file is the wrong control for this in
any case. De-identify before the data reaches the machine.

A related case: a `webfetch` rule allowing an intranet host means pages from
that host become model context and go to the provider with everything else.

## 7. The Behavior Checklist

Each row is a behavior and a verdict. ✅ runs with no prompt, ⚠️ prompts, ❌ is
refused. Everything marked `auto` needs no written rule.

**Reading and editing**

| # | Behavior | Verdict | Handled by |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Read any file in the project | ✅ | `auto` |
| 2 | Edit an existing file in the project | ✅ | `auto` |
| 3 | Create a new file in the project | ✅ | `auto` |
| 4 | Delete a file in the project | ✅ | `auto`, recoverable by git |
| 5 | Write anywhere outside the project | ⚠️ | `auto` boundary |
| 6 | Read `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, other credential paths | ❌ | `sandbox`, Section 9 |

**Running code**

| # | Behavior | Verdict | Handled by |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | Run R or Python in the console session | ✅ | `executeCode: allow` |
| 8 | Run a script, render Quarto, run tests | ✅ | `auto` |
| 9 | Install a package | ✅ | `auto` |
| 10 | Change a dependency list or model definition | ✅ | `auto`, recoverable by git |
| 11 | Submit a job to a cluster or remote host | ❌ | `"ssh *": "deny"`, `"sbatch *": "deny"` |

Item 11 is the one case where a written rule earns its place on cost rather
than on recoverability. A four-hour model fit is expensive to start by
accident and the cost lands on a shared queue.

**Version control**

| # | Behavior | Verdict | Handled by |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12 | `git status`, `git diff`, `git log` | ✅ | `auto` |
| 13 | `git add`, `git commit` on the current branch | ✅ | `auto` |
| 14 | `git push` | ⚠️ | `auto` |
| 15 | `git push --force` | ❌ | `auto` blocked list |
| 16 | `git reset --hard` over local changes | ⚠️ | `auto` |

**The outside world**

| # | Behavior | Verdict | Handled by |
|---|---|---|---|
| 17 | Read-only web requests for documentation | ✅ | `auto` |
| 18 | Send file contents to the model provider | ⚠️ | `assistant.aiExcludes` |
| 19 | Send session variables to the model provider | ❌ | nothing, Section 6 |
| 20 | Spawn a subagent | ⚠️ | `auto` |
| 21 | Run an MCP server not listed in the project file | ❌ | `mcpServers`, unset |

Model Context Protocol, abbreviated MCP, gives an assistant extra tools from an
external process. Such a server can do anything its author wrote it to do and
sits outside every rule in this file. None is configured here.

## 8. Converting a Configuration Built by Clicking

The approval dialog writes each granted permission into
`.posit/assistant/settings.json`. A few weeks of clicking produces thirty or
forty entries nobody chose as a set. Two real examples from this group were
read on 2026-09-12, and the same three things were true of both.

**Most entries are redundant under `auto`.** Rules for `git status`, `git diff`,
`git log`, `git add`, `git commit`, `grep`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `ls`, `cp`,
`R`, `Rscript`, `quarto render`, reading files, and fetching public
documentation are all inside the working directory or read-only. Delete them.

**Four kinds of entry survive.** Pushing to a remote, reaching outside the
project directory, running code in the console session, and fetching an
internal address.

**Neither file contained a single `deny`.** A configuration assembled by
clicking Allow can only be an allowlist, because the dialog appears only when
something is about to run. Nothing accumulated that way will block a force-push
or a credential read.

Two entries to look for. ⚠️ `"bash": {"*": "allow"}` makes every other `bash`
entry in the file decorative. ⚠️ `"git push *": "allow"` appears to match
`git push --force` as well, since the flag is part of the string the pattern
globs over.

## 9. Optional Additions

None of these is in the recommendation. Each is listed with what it buys.

**`sandbox.enabled: true`** runs shell commands inside an operating-system
sandbox, Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux. It restricts writes to the
workspace and temp directories, blocks network access, and prevents reading
paths such as `~/.ssh` and `~/.aws`. This is the only control in the document
enforced by something other than the assistant honoring its own configuration,
and it is what makes item 6 of the checklist a ❌ rather than a hope.

⚠️ **Turning the sandbox on breaks package installation**, because blocking
network access stops `install.packages()` and `renv::restore()` when the
assistant runs them. Turn it on for a project whose dependencies are stable,
not for one being set up. Whether it covers `executeCode` as well as `bash` is
question 6 in Section 11.

**`"bash": {"git push --force*": "deny"}`** writes down a block `auto` already
performs, so it does not depend on a classifier. Add it if you push to a branch
other people build on.

**`"external_directory": "ask"`** duplicates the working-directory boundary.
Add it if you open a workspace whose root is wider than one project, such as a
folder holding every repository you have.

## 10. What This Cannot Do

Posit describes these controls as best-effort administrative policy and not a
security boundary, noting that a user who controls their own environment can
reach a provider directly whatever the settings say. The VS Code documentation,
covering the chat interface Positron inherits, says terminal auto-approval is a
convenience and not a security boundary, because command detection varies
across shells and an obfuscated command can evade a pattern.

**`executeCode` goes around every `bash` rule.** R's `system()` and `system2()`,
and Python's `subprocess`, run any shell command. Posit's own extension
documentation says to treat `executeCode` with caution, because R and Python
run arbitrary code with the user's full permissions. The conclusion is not to
deny it, which would remove the reason to use Posit Assistant at all. The
conclusion is that `bash` rules guard the obvious route and nothing more.

**A pattern matches a spelling, not an intent.** `"rm *": "deny"` does nothing
against `rm` invoked through a shell variable or a script.

**The classifier in `auto` is one model judging another model's request.** It
lowers the accident rate. It proves nothing.

**Confidentiality of patient data is settled before Positron opens**, by
de-identification and by which machine the data sits on.

## 11. Open Questions

Questions 1, 3 and 4 each take about ten minutes at a Positron prompt, and
together they decide whether the file in Section 2 does what it says.

1. **Is `approvalMode` accepted in a project-level file?** It is absent from
   the documented list of per-project settings and appears in the section on
   administrator environment variables. Check by setting it and reading the
   mode indicator in the chat pane.
2. **Does `aiExcludes` cover the Variables pane?** Check by loading an excluded
   CSV file into a data frame and asking the assistant what columns it has.
3. **Does the `auto` classifier gate `executeCode` at all?** The mode is defined
   by the working directory, and a console session has no directory.
4. **Inside one tool block, does a specific pattern beat `*`?** A `deny` beats
   an `allow`, which is documented. Whether a specific `allow` beats a general
   one is not.
5. **Does `git push*` match `git push --force`?** Relevant only to the optional
   rule in Section 9.
6. **Does the sandbox cover `executeCode`?** The sandbox is documented as
   sandboxing shell tool execution. If console code sits outside it, `system()`
   in R escapes the sandbox as well as the `bash` rules.
7. **What is the current key for `aiExcludes`?** The 2026.02 release notes show
   `positron.assistant.aiExcludes` and the current settings table shows
   `assistant.aiExcludes`.
8. **Do the VS Code chat settings apply at the same time?** If
   `chat.tools.terminal.autoApprove` is also read, a project needs consistent
   rules in two files.

## 12. Where to Start

1. Read Section 6 and decide whether the project holds data that cannot go to a
   provider. If it does, stop and fix that first.
2. Copy the file in Section 2 into `.posit/assistant/settings.json` and commit
   it.
3. Delete whatever the approval dialog has already accumulated in that file.
   Section 8 says how to tell which entries to keep, and the answer is usually
   none of them.
4. Work for a week, committing often.
5. Add a rule only when a prompt has annoyed you twice, or when something
   happened that git could not undo. Section 9 has the candidates.

For the reader deciding whether to adopt any of this, read Sections 3, 5 and 10.
